opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Luis. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay, sure. I have a job later, but I have time now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for computers, not for framing. I don't use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes for me. What matters is if people keep building houses. If they build, I eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Take every job I can, send money to my family, keep a little for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Normal. Good.

S0.say: It's for computers, not for framing.
S0.think: Nothing changes. If people keep building houses, I eat.
S0.do: Takes every job he can, sends money to his family and keeps a little for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is good, people have time. Same as my work. You learn slow and you get good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think it touches me. Nobody does my work from a computer. Fewer beginners in offices, I don't know, maybe more young guys come to construction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working. Maybe teach the young guy on our crew to frame properly, so he has a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Not worried.

S1.say: Slow is good. You learn slow and you get good.
S1.think: It doesn't touch me. Nobody does my work from a computer.
S1.do: Keeps working and teaches the young guy on the crew to frame properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard for those families. Nobody should lose work like that. I'd pray for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My worry is, if office people lose their jobs, they don't buy houses. No houses, no framing. I get paid by the job, so I feel it the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look for steadier work with a bigger builder, not just job by job. Spend less, stop eating out. Keep sending money to my family. That I can't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little worried. Watching how much work comes.

S2.say: It's hard for those families. Nobody should lose work like that.
S2.think: If office people lose their jobs, they don't buy houses. I get paid by the job, so I feel it the same week.
S2.do: Looks for steadier work with a bigger builder, cuts spending, and keeps sending money to his family.
S2.feel: A little worried, watching how much work comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people at the top shouldn't keep everything. Workers build everything. Families need something too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices go up, maybe more building, maybe good. But if a lot of people lose jobs, maybe fewer buyers. I don't know which. My work goes up and down with the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take every job, weekends too. Try to save one month of money, which is hard with three kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'm strong. I can work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe good, maybe bad. Which do you think is more likely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'm not a money person. I watch how often the builder calls me. That tells me.

S3.say: The people at the top shouldn't keep everything. Workers build everything.
S3.think: Maybe more building, maybe fewer buyers. I don't know which. I watch how often the builder calls.
S3.do: Takes every job, weekends too, and tries to save one month of money.
S3.feel: Worried, but strong. He can work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a robot can't do what my hands do. A robot doesn't know when the wood is bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But I've seen videos of machines that build walls in a factory. If robots come to the site too, framing is one of the first things. It's repeat work. I have three kids and I send money to my family. There's no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the finish work, trim and cabinets, the fine work that's harder for a machine. Ask the builder straight if he plans to buy robots. Talk with my wife about her finding work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared for the kids. I don't sleep good thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said nobody does your work from a computer. Does that still hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From a computer, no. From a robot, maybe yes. That's different.

S4.say: A robot can't do what my hands do. It doesn't know when the wood is bad.
S4.think: Framing is repeat work, so it's one of the first things robots take. Three kids, family to support, no cushion.
S4.do: Learns finish carpentry, asks the builder straight about robots, and talks with his wife about her finding work.
S4.feel: Scared for the kids. Not sleeping well.
